tagline: Lagos on its lagoon and creeks — a megacity of 20 million where the water is the only way to beat the traffic.
summary: Nigeria's marine-mobility heart is Lagos, a megacity of ~20 million spread across islands, a lagoon and a maze of creeks — Lagos Island, Victoria Island, Ikoyi, Lekki and the mainland at Apapa and Ikorodu — linked by chronically gridlocked bridges. The Lagos State government has actively expanded ferry services (LASWA, the Lagos Ferry Services) precisely because the roads cannot cope. It is one of the world's largest and most congested water-commuter opportunities, where a clean fast tier addresses a genuine daily crisis.
why_marine_mobility: Lagos traffic is legendary, and the lagoon and creeks are the structural bypass the state is already investing in. Navier's Pioneer II flies the key commuter legs — Ikorodu to Lagos Island, the Victoria Island and Lekki crossings, the Apapa link — silent and zero-emission, upgrading an expanding but conventional ferry network, while the Quanta-LR range opens coastal connections along the Bight of Benin. The demand is vast, captive and growing.

demand_signals.label: Lagos megacity congestion
demand_signals.note: A metro of ~20 million with some of the world's worst road gridlock, where bridge bottlenecks make short trips take hours — a vast captive demand for any faster mode.

demand_signals.label: State-backed ferry expansion
demand_signals.note: LASWA and the Lagos Ferry Services are actively expanding routes and terminals across the lagoon and creeks — a clear government commitment to scaling water transport.

demand_signals.label: Victoria Island & Lekki waterfront
demand_signals.note: The Victoria Island, Ikoyi and Lekki districts concentrate Nigeria's highest-value commercial and residential demand on the waterfront, with marinas and creek frontage.

use_cases.body: A clean foiling commuter tier on the busiest lagoon crossings — Ikorodu to Lagos Island, the Victoria Island and Lekki links, the Apapa connection — bypassing hours of bridge gridlock.
On-demand premium hops across the Victoria Island, Ikoyi and Lekki creeks for the high-value business and residential market.
Coastal and creek leisure runs as the network matures, on silent zero-emission craft.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The Lagos lagoon-and-creek mesh — Ikorodu↔Lagos Island (~12 nm), Victoria Island↔Apapa (~4 nm), the Lekki and Ikoyi creek crossings (~2–6 nm) — sits inside the 70 nm all-electric range on sheltered lagoon and creek water off existing and expanding ferry terminals.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The lagoon network is Pioneer II territory; Quanta-LR hybrid range opens coastal line-haul along the Bight of Benin and toward the eastern creeks and delta without charging build-out.

transit_planning: For LASWA (Lagos State Waterways Authority) or a private operator: a clean foiling tier integrated with the state's expanding ferry terminals and routes, addressing a daily congestion crisis with silent, zero-emission craft, and the app relationship of a ride-hail brand like Yango.
competitive_landscape: Lagos has a growing but largely conventional ferry network (LASWA-licensed operators, government boats) competing with catastrophic road gridlock. Informal wooden boats serve many creek routes. There is no fast, clean, premium foiling tier — and the state's active expansion signals appetite for upgrades.
regulatory_note: Waterways are regulated by LASWA at state level and NIWA federally, with the Lagos State government strongly committed to expanding water transport as congestion relief. Terminal and route licensing through LASWA is the principal path; safety and standardisation are priorities the clean, stabilised Navier platform supports.
seasonality: The sheltered lagoon and creeks are navigable year-round, giving a weather-stable commuter profile; the rainy season (roughly April–October) brings heavier downpours and occasional squalls but limited sea-state disruption on the protected inland water, so the commuter case runs consistently.
